columns: id, fam (exercise family — its source file, checks and status labels are in `families`), unit, lesson, target (letter or word), phen (target phenomenon), prompt, answer, accepted (alternatives), distractors, hint (copy keys), expl (explanation), example, transcript (audio), pos, sense, level, locales, origin (generated/curated), findings (count), review (human-review flags)

evidence: not asked: fewer than three plausible distractors
not asked: fewer than three plausible distractors
not asked in this mode (no gap-fill for this word)
every pair of same-level words compared per locale; shared glosses are deduplicated by buildDailyQuestions at runtime

status_labels.AUTOMATED CHECKED: the checks named in `evidence` ran over this row in every locale it has text for
status_labels.MODEL-REVIEWED: the Korean side (prompt, answer, distractors, example, note) was read by the model on 2026-09-16; not a native-speaker review
status_labels.HUMAN REVIEW REQUIRED: no locale, Korean included, has been reviewed by a qualified native speaker

tensing.introduced: learning:sounds (소리가 만날 때), reached after every letter lesson
tensing.practised: word cards with a pronunciation note (WordIntro, WordDetailPage)
tensing.assessed: not assessed as a rule; the Level Test asks meanings and gap-fills

liaison.practised: not noted on cards by design (pronunciation.py NOTEWORTHY)

final-consonant neutralisation.practised: letter recognition and writing of the unit-11 syllables

human_review_summary.note: Heuristic hits: two glosses in one question that share a head word or contain each other. Each is listed once per locale and pair; the per-locale counts are in totals. Resolved hits are the ones the runtime never shows together (see dailyQuestions match dedupe, readingOptions sameMeaning, collideInAnyLocale).

rows.expl: Short for 조금, *a little* — but half its work is softening. Dropped into a request it takes the edge off: 도와주세요 is *help me*, 좀 도와주세요 is closer to *could you help me*. Korean speakers use it constantly for exactly that reason.

The adverb 그렇게 means so, in that way.

Textbooks list 당신 as polite "you", but in real speech it is mostly used between spouses — or, said to a stranger, it sounds confrontational. Koreans usually avoid "you" altogether: they use the person's name or title (선생님, 사장님) instead. Use 당신 with care.
